title: Options Pattern and Configuration Providers
description: Master the Options pattern for strongly typed settings, understand IOptions, IOptionsMonitor, and IOptionsSnapshot, and learn how to build custom configuration providers.

data.text: Modern applications need configuration from many sources: JSON files, environment variables, command-line arguments, Azure Key Vault, and more. ASP.NET Core's configuration system aggregates these sources into a single key-value hierarchy. The **Options pattern** sits on top of this system, giving you strongly typed classes to access settings instead of string-based dictionary lookups.

Using strongly typed options improves compile-time safety, enables validation, and makes your code easier to test. The framework provides three primary interfaces: `IOptions<T>` for singleton settings, `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` for scoped reloads, and `IOptionsMonitor<T>` for live updates when configuration changes.

An options class is a plain C# class with public properties that match the keys in your configuration file. The options system binds the configuration hierarchy to your class automatically. You can nest options using the colon separator in configuration keys or by using the `:` syntax in JSON.

data.title: Options class and appsettings.json binding
data.content: A strongly typed settings class bound from configuration.

data.text: Choosing the right interface depends on how often your configuration changes and whether you need fresh values within the same request. `IOptions<T>` is a singleton wrapper that reads configuration once at startup. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` reloads configuration on each request, which is useful during development. `IOptionsMonitor<T>` supports live reload without restarting the application.

rows: You need fresh values during development
You need to react to configuration changes without restarting

data.text: You can validate options at startup using data annotations or custom validators. If validation fails, the application throws an exception and refuses to start. This prevents running with invalid configuration. You can also use `IPostConfigureOptions<T>` to modify options after all configuration sources have been bound but before they are used.

data.title: Validating options with data annotations
data.content: Fail fast if required settings are missing or invalid.

data.title: Use ValidateOnStart() in Production
data.text: Without ValidateOnStart(), options validation happens lazily on the first request. This means your app can start with invalid configuration and only fail later. Always call ValidateOnStart() to catch configuration errors early.

Sometimes configuration lives outside JSON files or environment variables. You can write a custom configuration provider by implementing `IConfigurationProvider` and `IConfigurationSource`, or more commonly by using the `ConfigurationProvider` base class. Custom providers let you load secrets from Azure Key Vault, Consul, etcd, or a proprietary database.

terms.definition: A design pattern that uses strongly typed classes to represent groups of related configuration settings.
An options interface that provides live reload when configuration values change.
An abstraction that loads configuration key-value pairs from a custom source.

data.title: Options Pattern Summary
points: Options classes are plain C# classes bound to configuration sections.
IOptions<T> is singleton and reads once at startup.
IOptionsSnapshot<T> reloads per request for development scenarios.
IOptionsMonitor<T> supports live reload without restarting.
ValidateOnStart() fails fast if configuration is invalid.
Custom providers extend configuration to any data source.
data.takeaway: The Options pattern turns loose configuration keys into strongly typed, validated, and testable settings. Mastering it is essential for building maintainable, production-ready ASP.NET Core applications.
